messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Khalil's Cycle

Khalil was thirty years old when a drunk driver ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on a Tuesday evening in April. He remembered the sound first—the shriek of metal, the explosive crunch of glass—and then the sensation of his body being thrown sideways, his head snapping against the window. The other driver had smelled of whiskey and stale beer; Khalil had caught that acrid reek even through the airbag dust and his own shock. The paramedics told him later he was lucky. His left arm was broken in two places, his ribs badly bruised, but he had walked away from the hospital after three days. What he could not walk away from was the certainty that his body had betrayed him, that in a single moment of someone else's recklessness, everything he had relied upon—his steadiness, his competence, his ability to navigate the world safely—had been stripped away.

For the first few weeks, Khalil told himself the anxiety would fade. He had always been reliable, methodical—the kind of man who filed his own taxes meticulously and prided himself on never missing a deadline. At the Department of Revenue, where he worked as a tax inspector, colleagues had come to depend on his attention to detail and his calm under pressure. But by June, something had shifted. When a colleague's Honda Civic—the same model as the car that had hit him—pulled into the parking lot, Khalil felt his chest tighten. The shape of it, the angle of the headlights, triggered a cascade of images: the oncoming grille, the moment of impact, the taste of blood. He began to notice every car that resembled the one from the accident, and each sighting sent him spiraling into a state of high alert, his body tensed for danger that wasn't coming.

The triggers accumulated. One afternoon, someone spilled a glass of wine in the office break room, and the smell of alcohol—so similar to that night—sent Khalil into the bathroom where he locked himself in a stall for twenty minutes, his hands shaking. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own judgment, that his body might betray him again without warning, and this conviction made every potential trigger feel like a genuine threat. When his ex-wife called to discuss their divorce settlement, he found himself unable to focus on her words; instead, his mind raced with the certainty that he was no longer capable of managing the basic responsibilities that had once defined him as a professional and as a partner. The failure of his marriage, which had unraveled in the months following the accident as he withdrew into himself, seemed to confirm what he now knew to be true: he was fundamentally broken.

To manage the suffocating anxiety, Khalil developed a routine. Late at night, he would sit in his apartment with his phone, scrolling through games and social media for hours, losing himself in the blue glow until exhaustion finally pulled him under. The screen became his refuge from the intrusive images and the overwhelming sense of dread. During the day, he found that if he didn't eat, if he restricted his intake to coffee and the occasional piece of fruit, he could maintain a fragile sense of control—as if by limiting what entered his body, he could limit the chaos inside it. Most significantly, he stopped driving. The thought of being behind the wheel, or even sitting in a passenger seat, filled him with such primal terror that he began making excuses: he took the metro to work, asked colleagues for rides, and told his friends he preferred not to drive anymore. These avoidances quieted the immediate panic, but they also deepened his conviction that he was no longer capable, that the world had become fundamentally unsafe, and that his body was a liability he could not afford to trust.

Yet the relief was fleeting. The more Khalil avoided driving and vehicles, the more his hypervigilance intensified. Every unexpected sound—a car horn, a door slamming, a motorcycle passing on the street—sent him into a state of heightened alert. He would startle violently at ordinary noises, his nervous system locked in a state of perpetual threat detection. The longer he spent on his phone, lost in the escape of screens and games, the more his mind spiraled in the quiet moments between sessions: thoughts that he would never feel normal again, that something essential had been permanently damaged, that he could no longer be the person he once was. These dark convictions, born from the accident itself, seemed to justify his avoidance—why push himself if he was fundamentally changed?—yet they also fed the very hypervigilance and threat detection that made every day feel like an ordeal. By the time Khalil finally called a therapist in September, six months after the collision, he was working part-time because the commute had become unbearable, his weight had dropped noticeably, and he had not sat in a car voluntarily since the day of the accident. What he feared most was that this new version of himself—hypervigilant, avoidant, convinced of his own unreliability—was not temporary but permanent, a truth he could no longer escape.
